analysis.one_liner: Bars pharmacy benefit managers from pocketing the spread between what Medicaid pays for drugs and what pharmacies receive.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in December 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required Medicaid's contracts with pharmacy benefit managers to use "pass-through" pricing: every dollar the state pays for a drug would have to reach the pharmacy that dispensed it, with the middleman limited to a cost-based administrative fee. It would also have banned spread pricing — the practice of billing the state more than the pharmacy gets paid and keeping the difference — for federal reimbursement purposes, and expanded public reporting on drug prices, discounts, and dispensing fees. It was referred to committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid enrollees and the state taxpayers who fund Medicaid would benefit if drug payments that middlemen currently keep were passed through to pharmacies and states. Independent and community pharmacies would gain because they would receive the full ingredient cost and dispensing fee rather than reimbursement shaved down by a PBM. The public would also gain price data: the bill funds the national retail drug price survey at $5 million per year and requires publication of price concessions, dispensing fees, and pharmacy survey participation [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicaid patients, state taxpayers, and independent pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicaid contracts with pharmacy benefit managers and managed care plans to use pass-through pricing: payments for drugs are limited to ingredient cost plus a professional dispensing fee and must be passed in their entirety to the dispensing pharmacy, with the PBM or plan limited to a reasonable, cost-based administrative fee [S2][S3].

Prohibits spread pricing — billing Medicaid more than the pharmacy is paid and keeping the difference, including through post-sale fees and direct-and-indirect remuneration adjustments — by making any such spread unallowable for federal Medicaid matching payments [S3].

Forces PBMs and managed care entities to disclose to states and the federal government all drug-related costs and payments, including ingredient costs, dispensing fees, administrative fees, post-invoice fees, discounts, and rebates [S3].

Extends funding for the survey of retail pharmacy drug prices ($5 million per fiscal year) and requires public reporting of survey response rates, pharmacies out of compliance, price concessions, average dispensing fees, and separate acquisition costs for independent versus chain pharmacies [S3].

Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to report to Congress within a year on how specialty drugs are covered and reimbursed in Medicaid, including what states pay and how payment is set [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicaid managed care plans would lose the margin they currently keep between what Medicaid pays for drugs and what pharmacies receive; their compensation would be capped at a reasonable administrative fee. Federal taxpayers would fund the extended $5 million-a-year retail price survey, and pharmacies would bear a new obligation to respond to the price surveys [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicaid managed care plans

drawbacks.text: The bill extends federal funding for the retail drug price survey by $5 million for fiscal year 2020 and each year thereafter, a recurring federal cost [S3].

It requires any Medicaid-participating retail pharmacy receiving payments, fees, discounts, or rebates to respond to the price surveys, adding a compliance obligation for pharmacies large and small [S3].

The prohibition on spread pricing turns on what counts as a 'reasonable' administrative fee for the PBM, a standard that would require regulation to define and could invite disputes over where the line sits [S3].
The new pass-through rules apply only to contracts entered into or renewed 18 months or more after enactment, so savings and transparency would phase in slowly rather than immediately [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — closing a documented channel through which Medicaid dollars leak to middlemen, plus better public price data — outweigh the modest costs of $5 million a year for the survey and some compliance work for pharmacies and PBMs. The bill is narrow and transparency-focused rather than a broad drug price fix: it does not cap prices or address rebates from manufacturers, and its phased effective date would delay results. It also died without any committee analysis, so its administrative details were never tested in a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee the day after it was introduced, and no one ever gave it a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter, a Georgia Republican, introduced the bill on December 3, 2019, joined by Rep. Tony Cárdenas, a California Democrat, as its one cosponsor [S3][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on December 3, 2019, and to that committee's Subcommittee on Health on December 4 [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the bill sat in subcommittee until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicaid managed care plans are better off, because the spread-pricing margins the bill would have eliminated remained untouched. Pharmacies and state Medicaid programs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicaid managed care plans

sides.party_line_note: Only two members were ever attached — one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and no committee or floor votes were ever held, so no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (Express Scripts, CVS Caremark, OptumRx)
industries.note: The bill targets the core of the PBM business model in Medicaid: it would force every drug payment through to the pharmacy and let the PBM keep only a cost-based administrative fee, making any spread — including post-invoice fees and rebate adjustments — ineligible for federal matching funds [S3].

Plans responsible for covering outpatient drugs would have to comply with the same pass-through rules for pharmacy benefit services they provide or contract out, limiting their drug-related compensation to a reasonable administrative fee [S3].

Pharmacies would receive the full ingredient cost and dispensing fee instead of reimbursement reduced by a PBM's spread, though they would also face a new mandate to respond to the federal price surveys [S3].
The bill requires a government study of specialty drug reimbursement and whether specialty pharmacies should join the price survey, leaving their regulatory treatment open rather than settled [S3].
